# Public granaries and price stabilisation (ever-normal granary) (`ever_normal_granary`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/economy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Economy & finance (`economy`)
- Deps: helped by grain_storage_pest_control, price_mechanism_supply_demand
- Core idea: The state buys grain after good harvests, when it is cheap, stores it, and sells it at moderate prices after bad ones. Farmers are protected from ruinous gluts, town dwellers from famine prices, and the stock largely pays for itself because it is bought low and sold higher. It works if the stock is large relative to local trade, storage is dry, raised, ventilated and rotated every few years, purchases are made at market prices rather than by force, and stocks are counted and audited. Release grain early in a dearth and cap the sale price modestly, so private trade still has a reason to bring grain.
- Pitfalls:
  - Letting officials report full granaries that are empty or rotten: without audits and rotation the stock exists only on paper
  - Forcing farmers to sell to the granary below market price: they hide grain and plant less
  - Selling far below market: it drives private merchants out and the granary must then feed everyone
  - Building one central store: grain must be near the people who need it, before roads close
- History: egypt: pharaonic state granaries store tax grain; the Joseph story is literature, not a record; china: c. 400 BC – Li Kui's 'equalising purchases' in the state of Wei; 54 BC Geng Shouchang founds ever-normal granaries (changping cang) under Han Xuandi; Sui–Tang community 'charity granaries'; 18th c. Qing network holding millions of tonnes; rome: 2nd c. BC onwards – the annona: public purchase, storage and distribution of grain for the city of Rome; americas: 15th c. – Inca storehouses (qollqa) along roads hold maize, chuño and cloth; 1938 US Agricultural Adjustment Act implements an 'ever-normal granary' policy through price-support loans and reserves; europe: 14th–16th c. – city grain offices such as Florence's Abbondanza and the Venetian grain office
- Read:
  - Pierre-Étienne Will & R. Bin Wong, Nourish the People: The State Civilian Granary System in China, 1650–1850 (1991)
  - Amartya Sen, Poverty and Famines: An Essay on Entitlement and Deprivation (1981)
